title: Turf Removal & Replacement in Myrtle Beach | TIMELESS Grass & Greens
description: Replace worn or flooded turf on the Grand Strand. See where old turf can go in Horry and Brunswick counties, and when NC’s 30-foot buffer comes first.
h1: Replace worn or flooded turf on the Grand Strand.
lede: Take out turf that has worn through, sat under floodwater or never stopped puddling, from Shallotte to Conway. We look at the old turf and the base under it, then price removal, haul-away, base work and the new turf in writing before you commit.
wins: Flood damage in the base found before you commit
Where old turf can go on each side of the state line
When to ask North Carolina’s coastal office first

answer.question: What changes when you replace turf on the Grand Strand?
answer.answer: Three things. If the yard flooded, the base needs checking, not just the surface. Where the old turf can go depends on which county the yard is in. And on North Carolina waterfront, turf within the 30-foot shoreline buffer is a question for the state’s coastal office before anything else. Call 303-349-2368 for a free estimate.

blocks.h2: If floodwater sat on the turf, check what it left in the base.
paras: Hurricane Florence came ashore near Wrightsville Beach on 14 September 2018. It set South Carolina’s rainfall record for a tropical cyclone, 23.63 inches at Loris, and caused widespread flash flooding in Brunswick County, according to the National Hurricane Center’s Florence report.

In Conway, nearly 1,000 homes and businesses near the Waccamaw River flooded. On 26 September, twelve days after landfall, raw sewage flowed from the Conway Wastewater Treatment Plant into a tributary that feeds the river, the same report says.

So after a flood, tell us whether the water came from rain, the river or the tide, how many days it stood and what it left in the infill. Silt in the infill, or a base that has sunk or shifted, changes what can stay, and the written scope says which base work is included. The Conway page covers wet-yard questions in that city.

blocks.h2: The state line decides where old turf can go.
paras: In Horry County, the Solid Waste Authority’s disposal guide says its landfill at 1886 Highway 90 in Conway takes mixed construction debris, and asks for materials to be separated by type. Its C&D Processing Facility takes plastic, carpet and carpet padding for recycling. In Brunswick County, the county landfill in Bolivia takes construction debris from county property owners, residents and businesses, and only waste from Brunswick County. Turf pulled from a yard in Horry County can’t go there.

As of September 2026, artificial turf and used infill aren’t named in the SWA’s disposal guide, its C&D page or its fee schedule, or on Brunswick County’s accepted-items list. None of those pages says how old turf is classed. If you want it recycled, ask before it comes up rather than assuming a local option exists.

blocks.h2: On North Carolina waterfront, ask the state before turf goes back in the buffer.
paras: North Carolina’s coastal shoreline rule puts new development 30 feet back from the normal water level along estuarine and public trust shorelines, with listed exceptions. Landscaping is one. Turf isn’t named. In an August 2021 memo, Division of Coastal Management staff asked the Coastal Resources Commission to confirm their reading that turf doesn’t fall under that landscaping exception. The Commission then voted 10-1 to prohibit installing turf within the 30-foot buffer, Coastal Review reported in September 2021.

Staff came back to it in their annual rules review of November 2025, which lists the rule for a potential amendment clarifying that turf is not landscaping and is not permitted in the buffer. The rule text, checked in September 2026, still doesn’t mention turf, and it doesn’t say whether turf already in the buffer can be replaced. One exception covers development over an existing impervious surface that isn’t enlarged, and the rule doesn’t say whether old turf counts as one.

So if any turf you want to replace sits within 30 feet of the water, ask the DCM Wilmington District office, which serves Brunswick County, whether new turf can go in that spot and what permit it needs, before you plan the layout. How the wider coastal rules treat turf is set out in our state-line guide, and the Shallotte page explains how to confirm which local office reviews your parcel.

blocks.h2: Bring what shows the county, the flood and the shoreline.
paras: Tell us whether the yard is in Horry or Brunswick County and whether it sits inside a city. Send photos from during or after any flood. On North Carolina waterfront, bring any CAMA permit or DCM letter you have for the old turf.

On the free visit, we take measurements and look at the ground under the old turf. Work starts only after you approve a custom layout. The job covers site prep, a base suited to your soil, premium American-made turf laid with its seams and edges finished, infill and cleanup, and at the end we show you how to care for it. For the full scope, see our turf replacement service; the Grand Strand page lists the other turf we put in across the area.

faq.q: Will storm debris pickup take old turf?
faq.a: Ask first. The Horry County Solid Waste Authority’s Disaster Debris Management Plan (January 2022 update) asks residents to put storm debris along the right-of-way in separate piles, such as vegetative debris and construction debris, and notes that construction debris typically includes a lot of carpet. The plan never mentions turf. It lists a debris lead for each city in the county, so ask your city or the SWA which pile old turf belongs in.

faq.q: What if the turf is more than 30 feet from the water?
faq.a: It may still need a CAMA permit. In the same 2021 memo, DCM staff said turf anywhere in a coastal Area of Environmental Concern requires one, and that it may count toward the lot’s impervious surface limit after a case-by-case review, depending on how it’s installed. Ask the Wilmington District office whether your lot is in one before work starts.
